    1What an event dataset is

    An event dataset is a table where each row is one thing that happened, in one place, on one day: a protest, an airstrike, an attack on a clinic, the arrest of a journalist. The columns describe it: when, where, what, who was involved, how many people were harmed, and where the information came from.

    Once events are in a table, you can put them on a map and a timeline, count them and look for patterns: where attacks cluster, when they rise, which groups are involved. That is what this explorer does with your file.

    datelocationlatitudelongitudeevent_typenotessource
    2025-03-14Beni0.491129.4731Attack on a health facilityArmed men looted a health centre at night…https://…

    A made-up example row.

    2Decide what you are counting

    Before you search, write down in a few sentences what counts as an event for you. This keeps your data consistent, especially when several people work on it. Answer four questions:

    • What? For example: “Any physical attack on a health facility, health worker or ambulance, including looting and occupation by armed groups.”
    • Where and when? For example: “Ituri and North Kivu provinces, January to June 2025.”
    • What is one event? For example: “Everything one group does in one village on one day is one event.”
    • Which categories? A short, fixed list for the type of event, such as Killing, Abduction, Arson, Looting, Arrest. Always spell them the same way so they can be filtered and counted.

    Keep these rules in a “Read me” tab of your spreadsheet, and add to them each time you meet a case that doesn’t fit. Researchers call this document a codebook.

    3Set up your spreadsheet

    Use Google Sheets, Excel or LibreOffice. Keep it simple: one header row with column names, one row per event, no merged cells and no empty rows in between.

    ColumnWhat to writeNeeded?
    event_idA number for each event: 1, 2, 3…Recommended
    dateThe day it happened, written as year-month-day: 2025-03-14Yes
    date_endOnly if it lasted several days, or you only know it happened between two datesOptional
    country, admin1, locationCountry, then province or state, then village, town or siteRecommended
    latitude, longitudeWhere it happened, as decimal numbers: 0.4911, 29.4731 (how to find them)Yes
    geo_precisionHow exact the place is: 1 exact spot, 2 village or town, 3 district, 4 provinceRecommended
    event_typeOne of your fixed categoriesRecommended
    actor1, actor2Who did it, and to whom: “Unidentified armed group”, “Civilians”Optional
    fatalitiesNumber of people killed, as a number. Leave empty if unknown.Optional
    confidenceHow sure you are (see step 7)Recommended
    notesWhat happened, in one or two plain sentences, in your own wordsRecommended
    sourceLinks to every source, separated by a semicolon ;Recommended

    With these column names the explorer recognises your columns by itself, and the links in source become clickable in each event’s details. You can add any other column you need; it shows up in the details and can be used as a filter.

    Open the templates in Google Sheets (File › Import) or Excel. Each has one example row to show the format: delete it before you start.

    Or work right here. A new map timeline starts with these columns, plus a headline and an image, and you add events on the map or in the Sheet. A shared Google Sheet is still the better choice when several people collect events together.

    4Data that already exists

    Many organisations already record events. Check them first: they may cover what you need, or give you a starting list to verify and complete. Each one has its own definitions and each one misses things, especially in places with few journalists or little internet. Read its codebook before you count anything.

    Loads here means you can drop the downloaded file straight into this explorer.

    Armed conflict and political violence

    ACLEDLoads here
    Political violence, protests and riots worldwide, updated every week, with actors, notes, coordinates and named sources. Needs a free account.
    UCDP GEDLoads here
    Organised violence that killed at least one person, worldwide, with low, best and high death estimates and the sources used.
    GDELTLoads here
    Events coded by computer from world news every 15 minutes. Huge and noisy, with many duplicates: good for finding leads, not for counting.
    Global Terrorism DatabaseLoads here
    Terrorist attacks since 1970. Check which year it currently runs to.

    Attacks on aid, health care and education

    Aid Worker Security DatabaseLoads here
    Killings, kidnappings and serious attacks on aid workers since 1997.
    Insecurity Insight
    Attacks on health care, education and aid, often published on HDX as event lists with coordinates.
    WHO Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care
    Attacks on health care in selected emergencies, by country and date.
    GCPEA, Education under Attack
    Reports on attacks on schools, universities, students and teachers, and military use of schools.

    Explosive weapons, fires and damage

    Airwars
    Civilian harm from airstrikes and other explosive weapons, documented incident by incident with sources.
    Action on Armed Violence
    A worldwide monitor of explosive violence and the civilians it harms, based on English-language news.
    UNOSAT
    UN satellite analyses of damaged buildings and destroyed villages. Many are published on HDX as points you can map.
    NASA FIRMS
    Fires seen by satellites, with coordinates, within hours. Used to spot villages being burned, but most fires are farming or wildfires, so every lead needs checking. Download as CSV and pick acq_date as the date.

    People at risk

    Global Witness
    Killings and disappearances of land and environmental defenders, each year.
    Front Line Defenders
    Killings of and attacks on human rights defenders, in a yearly Global Analysis.
    Committee to Protect Journalists
    Journalists killed, imprisoned or missing since 1992, downloadable.
    Reporters Without Borders
    A barometer of journalists and media workers killed and detained.
    IOM Missing Migrants Project
    People who died or went missing on migration routes, with coordinates, downloadable.

    Displacement, civic space and the internet

    IOM Displacement Tracking Matrix
    Where displaced people are and where they came from, often down to camps and villages.
    IDMC
    Internal displacement figures by country, conflict and disaster.
    CIVICUS Monitor
    Regular updates on restrictions to protest, speech and association, country by country.
    Access Now #KeepItOn
    Internet shutdowns worldwide, by country and date.

    Hubs and investigators’ archives

    HDX, the Humanitarian Data ExchangeLoads here
    Thousands of datasets from UN agencies and NGOs, including many of the above. Files with HXL #tags load here directly.
    ReliefWeb
    Reports and situation updates from UN agencies and NGOs. Very good for searching (see the next step).
    Centre for Information Resilience, Bellingcat, Mnemonic
    Open-source investigation groups that publish verified, geolocated incidents and archives for crises such as Sudan, Myanmar, Ukraine, Syria and Yemen.

    5Find events with web searches

    When no dataset covers your topic, or you want to check one, you can build your own from news, reports and social media. Search engines become much more precise when you add a few search operators: short codes you type into the search box together with your words.

    Type thisTo getExample
    "…"Only pages with these exact words, in this order"health centre"
    ORPages with either word. Write it in capitals.looted OR burned
    ( )Groups words together(clinic OR hospital) attacked
    -Removes pages with this word-football
    site:Only one website, or one country’s websitessite:reliefweb.int site:.cd
    intitle:The word must be in the page titleintitle:massacre
    after: before:Only pages dated after or before a dayafter:2025-03-01 before:2025-03-08
    filetype:Only one type of file, like PDF reportsfiletype:pdf

    Example searches

    Attacks on health care in Sudan, from humanitarian reports:

    site:reliefweb.int (attack OR shelling) (hospital OR clinic OR "health facility") Sudan after:2025-01-01

    Local-language news. In eastern DR Congo most reporting is in French:

    "centre de santé" (attaqué OR pillé OR incendié) Ituri after:2025-01-01 before:2025-02-01

    One trusted local outlet, one week at a time:

    site:radiookapi.net Beni ADF after:2025-03-01 before:2025-03-08

    Journalists attacked in one Mexican state, in Spanish:

    (periodista OR reportero) (asesinado OR atacado OR desaparecido) Sinaloa after:2025-06-01 before:2025-07-01

    Villages set on fire in one region of Myanmar, leaving out wildfires:

    (village OR villages) (torched OR burned OR "set fire") Sagaing -wildfire after:2025-01-01

    Official reports that list incidents in tables:

    filetype:pdf "situation report" Tigray "health facility"

    Tips to find more

    • Search short periods. A search engine shows at most a few hundred results, so a search over a whole year hides most events. Go week by week, or month by month, with after: and before:.
    • Search place by place. Make a list of the towns and villages in your area and run the same search for each one.
    • Use the local languages and the words people there use: local names of armed groups, nicknames, and different spellings of places (Beni, Béni).
    • Use the News tab, then Tools to pick a date range and sort by date. Look past the first page of results.
    • Try other search engines. Bing, Yandex (strong for Russian-language sources) and Baidu (Chinese) return different results.
    • Search social media. X’s advanced search accepts since:2025-03-01 until:2025-03-08. Telegram channels are central in many conflicts. Treat every post as a claim until you have verified it.
    • Keep watching. Turn your best searches into Google Alerts so new results arrive by email.

    6Collect and preserve what you find

    Keep a search log: a second tab where every useful result gets a row, before you decide whether it describes an event. It shows how you found things, lets someone else repeat your work, and stops you reading the same article twice.

    ColumnWhat to write
    found_onThe day you found it
    queryThe exact search you typed
    url, archive_urlThe link, and the link to your saved copy
    outlet, published, headline, languageWho published it, when, the title, the language
    relevantYes or no, according to your definition
    event_idWhich event in your event tab it describes

    Save a copy of every page as soon as you find it. Pages are edited and deleted all the time, social media posts most of all.

    • Paste the link into “Save Page Now” on the Wayback Machine, and copy the archive link into archive_url. archive.today can save many pages the Wayback Machine can’t.
    • For posts and videos, also save a screenshot or PDF with the link and the date visible, and download the media where that is legal and safe.
    • If your work may be used as evidence, follow the Berkeley Protocol on Digital Open Source Investigations. It explains how to collect, preserve and verify online information so it holds up. Tools such as Hunchly record every page you visit automatically.

    7Turn articles into events

    1. Check it against your definition. If the article doesn’t describe an event you count, mark it “no” in the search log and move on.
    2. Find the day of the event, not the day of publication. “On Sunday”, in an article published on Tuesday 18 March 2025, means 2025-03-16. If you can only narrow it down, put the first possible day in date and the last in date_end.
    3. Look for the event in your sheet first. Several articles often describe the same event. Don’t add a second row: add the new link to the source column (after a ;) and improve the notes.
    4. Fill in the columns. Write the notes in your own words and say who claims what: “According to local civil society, …”.
    5. Be careful with numbers. When sources disagree about how many people died, put the lowest credible number in fatalities and describe the range in the notes. Leave it empty if nobody knows: 0 means you know that nobody died.
    6. Record how sure you are in confidence, with a few fixed words. For example: Confirmed (two or more independent sources), Single source, or Claim (only one party says so).

    Test your rules: ask a colleague to turn the same 20 articles into events on their own, then compare. Where your results differ, your definitions need to be clearer.

    8Add coordinates

    The map needs a latitude and a longitude for each event: two decimal numbers, like 0.4911 and 29.4731. Latitude is negative south of the equator; longitude is negative west of Greenwich (the Americas, most of West Africa).

    • Google Maps: find the place, right-click on it and click the two numbers at the top of the menu to copy them. The first is the latitude, the second the longitude.
    • OpenStreetMap: right-click on the place and choose “Show address”; the coordinates appear on the left. It often has villages that Google Maps lacks.
    • GeoNames: finds places under many spellings and in many languages, useful for small villages.
    • Check it is the right place. Many villages share a name. Compare with the district or province named in the article.
    • Only as exact as you know. If you only know the district, use the centre of the district and set geo_precision to 3. Never make a place look more exact than it is.

    9Check, export and load

    • Dates are written as 2025-03-14. 03/04/2025 can mean 3 April or 4 March.
    • Coordinates use a decimal point, not a comma: 0.4911, not 0,4911. Excel in some languages uses commas.
    • Latitudes are between -90 and 90, longitudes between -180 and 180. Swapped columns put events in the wrong place, often in the sea.
    • One header row, no merged cells, no totals at the bottom.

    Save it as CSV. Google Sheets: File › Download › Comma-separated values. Excel: File › Save As › CSV UTF-8 (this keeps accents and non-Latin letters). LibreOffice: File › Save As › Text CSV, with character set UTF-8.

    Load it here. Drop the CSV on the start page. The explorer shows which column it thinks is which; fix anything it got wrong and open the map. Dots in odd places usually point to a typo.

    Fix mistakes in the Sheet. Switch to the Sheet view to correct a date, place an event on the map or add a row, without going back to your spreadsheet. Rows marked ! won’t show on the map, and the mark tells you why. Download the CSV to take your changes back to Google Sheets or Excel.

    10Tell the story with a map timeline

    A map timeline walks readers through your events one at a time: the map moves to each place while a card shows what happened, with a headline, an image and the sources. It is built to sit inside a news article, like a chart. Open any dataset and choose Map timeline at the top of the screen, or start one from scratch on the start page.

    Choose and write

    • Pick the events that carry the story. Ten to forty is plenty. Take the rest out with Leave out on their card, or filter them in Explore and choose Make a map timeline.
    • Write on the graphic itself. Click the title, the subtitle, a headline or the text to type in it. Write each headline as a plain sentence saying who did what, where: “Armed men loot the health centre in Beni”, not “Tragedy strikes”.
    • In the text, say who claims what, what is confirmed and what is still disputed. Keep the source links: readers and editors will check them.
    • Use text cards for context or a turning point: a card with no place, between two events.
    • Fill in the source and credit line under the map, and use the introduction on the cover to say what the map leaves out.

    Images

    • Only use images you have the right to use, and credit them under the image.
    • Think before showing dead or injured people, and blur or leave out faces of victims, witnesses and bystanders who could be put at risk.
    • Uploaded images are made smaller and re-saved without their hidden data, such as the GPS location where a photo was taken. They are stored inside your project and the files you share.
    • An image link loads the picture from the other website each time someone opens your graphic, which tells that site who is looking, and the picture disappears if the site removes it. Upload a copy when you can.

    Put it in an article

    • Choose Share › Embed the map timeline in an article. The explorer checks what’s missing, shows the graphic at phone, article and wide sizes, and makes one small web page with everything inside: data, map, images and code. Readers’ browsers load nothing from other websites.
    • Only the columns the graphic shows go into that file, and events you left out never do. Tick Blur locations to round coordinates to about 1 km where exact places could lead someone to a home or a hiding place.
    • Upload the file where your publication can link to it: your website’s file storage, or GitHub Pages (create a repository, upload the file, then turn on Pages in the repository’s settings).
    • Paste the file’s address in the Share window, copy the embed code, and paste it into your article where your publishing system accepts HTML. With automatic fitting, the graphic takes the height it needs at every width.
    • Open the article on a phone and step through every card before you publish: most readers will see it there.

    Keep your work

    • Projects save themselves in this browser as you work, and are listed on the start page. Browsers can clear what they store, so download a Project file from Share often.
    • A project file holds your rows, settings and images. Send it to a colleague, and open it by dropping it on the start page. The graphic’s file can be dropped there too, to edit it again.

    11Stay safe and do no harm

    • Protect yourself. Use a separate browser profile and separate accounts for research. Watch without interacting: don’t like, follow, comment or send messages, and remember that some sites show who viewed a profile.
    • Protect others. Only record the names of victims, witnesses or sources when you truly need them, and keep the spreadsheet private. Before you publish a map, ask whether it could put anyone in danger.
    • Check images before you publish. Faces, uniforms, number plates and street signs can identify people. Photos from phones often carry the exact place they were taken: upload them here, which removes that data, rather than sharing the original files.
    • Protect your wellbeing. Violent images affect everyone. Turn off autoplay, view images small or in black and white, take breaks, and talk with colleagues about what you have seen.
    • Be honest about gaps. Your dataset shows what was reported and found, not everything that happened. Places without internet, journalists or free media look quieter than they are. Say so when you share your results.
